Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
What she saw first was a moving shadow. In the trees that bordered the meadow, among their dark trunks, something moved. She heard nothing to alarm—not over the rush of water and the sweep of wind—but she saw a dark, crouched shape moving. The shadow, no more than a darker darkness in the night, crept out from the mass of trees, crept low across the long grass towards the docking place. No man of the village would move so. A man of the village, come out to check a hastily secured boat, would carry a light. He would come along the path that ran from the village through the Innyard, the path she stood on. No fisherman would be setting off, not at this hour, not on a moonless night when all the stars shining together couldn't penetrate the dark, windy air.

Birle stood motionless, watching. She herself ought not to be out in the night. Da and Nan would not be pleased to know how she had left her small sisters asleep in the bed they shared, pulled on her skirt and overshirt, and latched the door stealthily behind her to tiptoe past the room where her brothers slept, past the room where Da and Nan slept, down the broad staircase and across the empty public room. In the kitchen, where the banked fire glowed in its ashes, she had put on her boots and taken her cloak from its hook. The dogs, if they heard anything, knew her steps and took no alarm. Da and Nan, if they knew, would be mightily displeased, and they would lay angry words across her shoulders. Aye, they were counting the days left to the spring fair, when they would have her married and gone from their care. Aye, and Birle was counting them too.

The shadow was human, she had no doubt of that. Only a man or woman would move so, hunched over, gliding along the edge of the river like a beast on the hunt among the long grasses. Watching, Birle let the wind urge her down the path to the docking place. Whatever else, the shadow was up to nothing lawful.

Soaking spring rains had turned the path to mud. Her boots made squishing sounds, so she stepped off the path into the grass. As soundlessly as the shadow before her, but more swiftly, she approached the river.

She should return to the sleeping Inn, she knew that, and rouse her brothers. At the least, she should turn and call out an alarm, to set the dogs barking. But the mystery of the intruder, like the mystery of the night which had called her from sleep, kept her from doing what she ought.

AnswerD: have walked through the Innyard.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
The First Lighthouse

It was in ancient Egypt, around 2300 years ago, that the great Pharaoh Ptolemy I Soter ordered plans to be drawn up for what was to be the world's first lighthouse. It was to be built on the island of Pharos, one-and-a-half kilometres off the coast of the city of Alexandria. The purpose of the Lighthouse of Pharos, as it became known, was to protect ships coming into the dangerous waters of the Alexandria harbour. Standing more than 110 metres high and built out of white marble, the Lighthouse of Pharos was so impressive that it became one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

In those days, as nearly the tallest building around, it must have had the best views in the world! (The pyramids at Giza were taller, but it was forbidden to climb them—as it still is now.)

The design of the lighthouse was very different to those we see today; it was built in three stages. The bottom level was over 60 metres high and more than 30 metres square. It looked like a huge box. On top of the box was an octagonal tower about 27 metres high with each of its eight sides more than 18 metres wide. And on top of the tower was a cylinder over seven metres high. During the day, the sun reflected off mirrors made of highly-polished bronze and at night, the lighthouse was lit by fires. It was said that the light from the Lighthouse of Pharos could be seen for more than 56 kilometres out to sea.

Incredibly, almost 700 years after it collapsed in an earthquake, the fame of the Lighthouse of Pharos lives on. In October 1994, Frenchman Dr Jean-Yves Empereur was asked by the Egyptian Supreme Council of Antiquities to investigate an area beneath the sea, just outside Alexandria's eastern harbour. In 1995 he took a team of divers, topographers, Egyptologists and photographers with him and started to mark, chart and illustrate approximately 1000 archaeological artefacts found on the bottom of the sea.

Apart from locating enormous blocks of stone and fragments from columns, the excavators also found sphinxes, parts of obelisks and inscribed blocks, all of which the excavators believed most likely belonged to the Lighthouse of Pharos. Even more exciting was the discovery that some of these building materials were much older than the Lighthouse of Pharos.

The Egyptian authorities are planning to build a modern version of the lighthouse on the very same spot at Pharos. This lighthouse will be made of concrete with glass walls and will be 145 metres high. The walls will reflect the sun by day and a beacon will cast its light at night.
QuestionText: What can be assumed about the materials that went into building the Lighthouse of Pharos?
AnswerA: The action of the sea had preserved the building materials.
AnswerB: The Lighthouse of Pharos consisted of 1000 pieces of building material.
AnswerC: The building materials from the Lighthouse of Pharos's octagonal tower were fully recovered.
AnswerD: Some of the building materials were recycled from older buildings.

The Gap in the Arch
All through the winter of 1930, Molly Fraser walked to the end of her street in North Sydney every afternoon to look at the bridge. For years it had been growing out from both sides of the harbour, two great steel arms reaching towards each other across the water. Each day the gap between them looked a little smaller.
Molly's father was a rigger on the bridge. He left before dawn and came home with grease on his hands and stories in his head. He told her about the creeper cranes that crawled along the top of each half-arch, lifting steel into place. He told her about the riveting gangs, too: one worker heated the rivets in a little furnace until they glowed, then tossed them through the air to a catcher who snatched them in a metal cup.
'What stops the two halves from falling into the harbour?' Molly asked one night.
'Cables,' said Dad. 'Huge steel cables anchored in tunnels in the rock. They hold each half back, like a hand on a dog's collar.'
In August, the workers began to let the cables out, slowly, a little each day. The two half-arches tilted forward, inch by careful inch. Half of Sydney seemed to be watching.
Then, late on the night of the nineteenth, the two halves touched. Molly heard the news from a neighbour running down the street, shouting. The next morning she raced to the corner. The ragged gap had gone. Instead, one enormous arch curved across the sky, steel grey against the blue, as if it had always been there.
That evening, Dad came home tired but smiling. Molly could hear the ships in the harbour hooting, and the clatter, clang and rattle of the riveters still working in the distance.
'Is it finished?' she asked.
'Not yet,' said Dad, ruffling her hair. 'But the hardest part is done. Now they can hang the road.'

The Bird Behind the Mud Wall
In the forests of Asia and Africa lives a bird with one of the strangest nesting habits on Earth. Hornbills are large birds with huge curved beaks, and many species have a hollow helmet called a casque on top. But it is what happens inside their nests that truly amazes scientists.
When it is time to lay her eggs, a female hornbill chooses a hollow in a tall tree. She climbs inside, and then she does something remarkable: she seals herself in. Using mud, chewed fruit and her own droppings, she plasters the entrance until only a narrow slit remains. In some species, her mate brings mud to help.
For the next few weeks, sometimes for several months, the female stays shut inside. In many species she sheds her flight feathers while she is there. She lays her eggs, keeps them warm and cares for the chicks when they hatch.
The wall works like a fortress. Snakes, monkeys and other hungry animals cannot reach the eggs through such a tiny gap. But it also means the female depends completely on her partner.
The male's task is exhausting. Day after day, he flies back and forth through the forest, collecting fruit, insects and small animals. He swallows the food, carries it to the nest, then brings it back up and passes it, piece by piece, through the slit to the female's waiting beak. A male may make dozens of trips in a single day. If something happened to him, his family would be in serious trouble.
When the chicks are larger and the nest is crowded, the female breaks out through the wall. In some species, the chicks then rebuild the seal by themselves and stay safely inside until they are ready to fly.
Sadly, many hornbills are now threatened because the giant trees they need are being cut down. Without old trees with big hollows, there is nowhere to build these remarkable mud-walled nurseries.
